guidance:
Work only with the content of Table 1. Use other text only to understand layout, not as a source of values.

1) Columns and headers
- Read the full header row (or rows) from left to right before creating any cells.
- Add every explicit data column header to `columns` (e.g., each group, arm, timepoint, or statistic column). Do not invent combined or "total" columns unless they are printed as headers.
- For multi-level headers (a top header spanning several subheaders), treat only the lowest-level headers as data columns. Build each `column_label` by combining the higher-level group and the leaf header into a single string (e.g., "Group: Leaf").
- The leftmost label column may have its own heading. If present, include that heading in `columns` but never create data cells for it; the contents of that column are represented via `row_label` and `row_group`.
- Every `column_label` that appears in any cell must appear exactly once in `columns`. Do not create extra or duplicate column names.

2) Row groups vs. row labels
- Use the leftmost column to identify structure:
  • Section/category headings: often styled differently, spanning columns, or followed by several related rows.
  • Data rows: aligned with values in data columns.
- Treat each section/category heading as a `row_group`. All subsequent data rows belonging to that section use that heading verbatim as `row_group` and their own label text as `row_label`.
- Rows that clearly start a new section without a separate heading (e.g., the table begins with data rows) should have `row_group` = null.
- If a section heading itself has values in the data columns on the same line, represent that line with `row_group` equal to the heading text and `row_label` = null.
- Do not swap roles: `row_group` is the broader category or section; `row_label` is the specific item within that section. Do not treat item names as groups or groups as labels.
- When the same section or row label appears more than once, reuse the text exactly so that grouping remains consistent.

3) Building cells
- A cell corresponds to one non-empty intersection of a data row and a data column.
- For every visible numeric or textual entry in the body of Table 1, create exactly one cell object with fields: `row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`, `value`.
- Copy `value` exactly as printed, including spaces, punctuation, parentheses, ranges, units, percent signs, plus/minus signs, and textual markers such as "N/A" or dashes when they appear as values.
- A printed zero is a real value and must be included.
- Do not create cells for blank entries. Never infer, calculate, or move values between rows or columns.

4) Avoid missing, extra, and duplicate cells
- Work row by row: for each data row, scan across all data columns and ensure that every non-empty entry is represented once in `cells`.
- Do not create cells for rows that are purely headers or section titles and have no data values.
- Do not add derived totals, summary statistics, or extra subgroup columns that are not explicitly part of the table header.
- Each combination of (`row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`) must be unique. If the layout looks repetitive (e.g., similar text appears twice), check carefully whether it is a different position in the table or the same position; only emit a cell when there is a distinct data entry.

5) Consistency of strings
- Use the table text verbatim for `table_title`, `columns`, `row_group`, `row_label`, and `column_label`, preserving spelling, capitalization, and symbols.
- Ensure that every `column_label` used in `cells` matches exactly one entry in `columns`, and that section headings used as `row_group` are consistent across all related rows.
